topic.title: Never say 'wedding'
topic.claim: Every family planning a wedding learns to call it a 'small family function' on the phone, because the word wedding changes the quote.
topic.moment: Your cousin calls the caterer and says 'just a get-together, around 150 people'.

turn.believed: Vendors charge more because weddings are more work.
turn.actually: Vendors charge more because families won't bargain on the most emotional day of their lives.

topic.because: People don't want to look cheap at a wedding, and vendors know it. The word itself signals a buyer who won't walk away.
topic.payoff: If saying one word adds a lakh, the lakh was never for the work.
topic.behaviour: Families hide the occasion while booking venues, decor and photographers to get normal rates.
topic.mechanism: Vendors price on how little the buyer will push back, and wedding buyers push back least.
topic.group: Young adults helping plan their own or a sibling's wedding
topic.send_to: The sibling who is booking the venue next month.
topic.why_now: Wedding season is on, and every family is calling vendors right now.

score.why: Calling a wedding a 'get-together' to dodge the quote. It's a family arrangement nobody names, and the closing line stings.

topic.villain: a wedding-pricing norm that charges more to buyers who won't walk away

Wrong: 'It is currently wedding season in India.'. What's true: On 2026-11-07 the Hindu wedding season has not started. Chaturmas, when weddings are traditionally avoided, ends on Dev Uthani Ekadashi, which is Friday 20 November 2026 (some observe it on 21 November). The first main wedding muhurats come after that, around 21 to 26 November, and run into December. 2026 has an extra month (Adhik Maas), which pushes the season later than in 2025, when it started around 1 November. Some weddings still happen in early November in regions or communities that don't follow the Chaturmas restriction, so a claim of a general season would be wrong, not just early. I found no CAIT or other trade-body report of a 2026 season starting before 20 November. The post could say instead that the season is about to begin, or starts on 20 November..

mechanism.broken_premise: None of the premises is demonstrably false. Two need caveats. Premise 1 sounds universal, but the best evidence comes from US mystery-shopper tests, and only about a quarter of quotes rose when the event was called a wedding. I found no comparable study of Indian caterers. Premise 2 leaves out some legitimate non-haggling reasons for a higher wedding quote: peak muhurat dates that turn away other bookings, a higher service standard (more staff, live counters, cake-cutting or service fees), and the risk of something going wrong at a one-time event. None of that is cost of the food. Tax doesn't explain the gap either. Under Notification 11/2017-CT(Rate), as amended by 20/2019, GST on outdoor catering depends on the venue (specified premises or not), not on what the event is called. A 150-plate order with the same menu, venue and date carries the same tax whether it's a 'family function' or a shaadi.
mechanism.actual_mechanism: Some vendors charge more based on the occasion, a practice called the 'wedding tax'. The word 'wedding' tells them the buyer has a fixed date, is emotionally invested and is unlikely to switch vendors, so they can charge more than for an identical spec. Mystery-shopper tests found it in a minority of cases, not across the board: Consumer Reports saw higher wedding quotes in just over a quarter of cases, and CHOICE in Australia found it at 3 of 6 venues. Part of a real wedding premium can also come from date scarcity and extra service rather than haggling power. When the menu, headcount, date and venue truly match, though, the extra amount is buyer-based pricing, not cost.

Lists the GST rate for wedding and event catering by venue: 5% outside specified premises, 18% with ITC at specified premises. The rate depends on the venue, not the type of occasion.

ledger.text: Caterers/wedding vendors quote a materially higher per-plate price for an identical menu, hall, and date once the word 'wedding' (or 'shaadi') is used instead of a generic term like 'small get-together,' because they know couples won't negotiate or walk away from vendors on their own wedding day — meaning the price difference reflects the word used, not any difference in food, staffing, or service.
ledger.sentence: Say wedding on the phone and the quote jumps. ... Same menu, same hall, same date. The food didn't change. The word did. ... And the vendor knew that before you picked up the phone.

ledger.text: The writer has personally heard someone describe their own wedding as a 'small get-together' while saying it with a completely straight face.
ledger.sentence: I've heard "small get-together" said with a completely straight face.

mechanism.broken_premise: None. Every falsifiable premise holds: a matched-service test (identical event, same date/menu/venue) does produce higher quotes once 'wedding' is used, and the driver is willingness-to-pay/inelastic demand, not a cost difference.
mechanism.actual_mechanism: Wedding vendors price on willingness-to-pay, not cost. In a controlled test where the only variable changed was calling the event a 'wedding' versus a non-wedding party of identical date, size and service, a meaningful share of vendors quoted the wedding higher — Consumer Reports found 28% did, with examples like photography at $300/hr vs $150/hr for the same afternoon. Because couples face social pressure, a fixed date and emotional stakes, demand is inelastic and they won't walk or haggle, so the label itself is the pricing signal the vendor responds to.

sources.quote: In more than a quarter of cases—28 percent—vendors quoted us prices that were higher for the wedding than for the anniversary party.
Angel Wings Photography in Atlanta charged $300 per hour for a Saturday wedding but $150 per hour for an identical anniversary party.
catering costs jumped from $900 to $2,700 when the event type changed from corporate to wedding—same date, location, time, and guest count (65 people).

It's for the one day you'd feel cheap counting rupees in front of everyone.

[end card] Read it again before you call the first caterer.
Send to the sibling booking the venue next month, before they say the word out loud.

c6.correct: On 2026-11-07 the Hindu wedding season has not started. Chaturmas, when weddings are traditionally avoided, ends on Dev Uthani Ekadashi, which is Friday 20 November 2026 (some observe it on 21 November). The first main wedding muhurats come after that, around 21 to 26 November, and run into December. 2026 has an extra month (Adhik Maas), which pushes the season later than in 2025, when it started around 1 November. Some weddings still happen in early November in regions or communities that don't follow the Chaturmas restriction, so a claim of a general season would be wrong, not just early. I found no CAIT or other trade-body report of a 2026 season starting before 20 November. The post could say instead that the season is about to begin, or starts on 20 November.

mechanism.broken_premise: None of the premises is demonstrably false. Two need caveats. Premise 1 sounds universal, but the best evidence comes from US mystery-shopper tests, and only about a quarter of quotes rose when the event was called a wedding. I found no comparable study of Indian caterers. Premise 2 leaves out some legitimate non-haggling reasons for a higher wedding quote: peak muhurat dates that turn away other bookings, a higher service standard (more staff, live counters, cake-cutting or service fees), and the risk of something going wrong at a one-time event. None of that is cost of the food. Tax doesn't explain the gap either. Under Notification 11/2017-CT(Rate), as amended by 20/2019, GST on outdoor catering depends on the venue (specified premises or not), not on what the event is called. A 150-plate order with the same menu, venue and date carries the same tax whether it's a 'family function' or a shaadi.
mechanism.actual_mechanism: Some vendors charge more based on the occasion, a practice called the 'wedding tax'. The word 'wedding' tells them the buyer has a fixed date, is emotionally invested and is unlikely to switch vendors, so they can charge more than for an identical spec. Mystery-shopper tests found it in a minority of cases, not across the board: Consumer Reports saw higher wedding quotes in just over a quarter of cases, and CHOICE in Australia found it at 3 of 6 venues. Part of a real wedding premium can also come from date scarcity and extra service rather than haggling power. When the menu, headcount, date and venue truly match, though, the extra amount is buyer-based pricing, not cost.

ledger.text: Caterers/wedding vendors quote a materially higher per-plate price for an identical menu, hall, and date once the word 'wedding' (or 'shaadi') is used instead of a generic term like 'small get-together,' because they know couples won't negotiate or walk away from vendors on their own wedding day — meaning the price difference reflects the word used, not any difference in food, staffing, or service.

mechanism.broken_premise: None. Every falsifiable premise holds: a matched-service test (identical event, same date/menu/venue) does produce higher quotes once 'wedding' is used, and the driver is willingness-to-pay/inelastic demand, not a cost difference.
mechanism.actual_mechanism: Wedding vendors price on willingness-to-pay, not cost. In a controlled test where the only variable changed was calling the event a 'wedding' versus a non-wedding party of identical date, size and service, a meaningful share of vendors quoted the wedding higher — Consumer Reports found 28% did, with examples like photography at $300/hr vs $150/hr for the same afternoon. Because couples face social pressure, a fixed date and emotional stakes, demand is inelastic and they won't walk or haggle, so the label itself is the pricing signal the vendor responds to.

sources.quote: In more than a quarter of cases—28 percent—vendors quoted us prices that were higher for the wedding than for the anniversary party.
Angel Wings Photography in Atlanta charged $300 per hour for a Saturday wedding but $150 per hour for an identical anniversary party.
catering costs jumped from $900 to $2,700 when the event type changed from corporate to wedding—same date, location, time, and guest count (65 people).

paragraphs: Say wedding on the phone and the quote jumps.
slides.why_swipe: Why the careful wording on a simple call?

paragraphs: The rate comes back normal. Reasonable, even.
You figure the real wedding prices are just for the real work: more staff, late nights, extra rounds of starters going out.
slides.why_swipe: So is the markup actually about the work?

paragraphs: A week later, someone on the call lets "shaadi" slip.
Suddenly the per-plate climbs. Same menu, same hall, same date.
**The food didn't change. The word did.**
slides.why_swipe: If nothing changed, what are they charging for?

paragraphs: Here's the part nobody books for. On that day, you won't haggle over 20 rupees a plate with your chachi standing right there.
You won't walk away. And the vendor knew that before you picked up the phone.
I've heard "small get-together" said with a completely straight face.
slides.why_swipe: So what is the extra lakh really buying?

paragraphs: The extra lakh was never for the biryani.
It's for the one day you'd feel cheap counting rupees in front of everyone.
